Zurich (German: Zürich; Alemannic German: Züri; see below) is the largest city in Switzerland and the capital of the canton of Zurich. It is in north-central Switzerland, at the northwestern tip of Lake Zurich. As of the end of 2025, the municipality had a population of 440,935, while the urban area was home to 1.45 million people (2020), and the Zurich metropolitan area had a total population of 2.1 million (2020). Zurich is a hub for railways, roads, and air traffic. Both Zurich Airport and Zurich's main railway station are the largest and busiest in the country.
Zurich is a cosmopolitan city. While German is the official language and Zurich German, the most widely spoken variety, the use of both German and Swiss German at home is steadily declining, whereas the use of English has increased by 60% over ten years, reaching 14% of the population in 2024, and 40% of Zurich residents speak English at work.
Evidence of early, sparse settlements in the area dates back more than 6,400 years, indicating human presence prior to the establishment of the town. Permanently settled for over 2,000 years, Zurich was eventually founded by the Romans, who called it Turicum. During the Middle Ages, Zurich gained the independent and privileged status of imperial immediacy and, in 1519, became a primary centre of the Protestant Reformation in Europe under the leadership of Huldrych Zwingli.
The city has a large presence of operations from 7 of the 10 globally leading AI companies. This, along with the presence of ETH Zurich, makes the city a significant location in developing technologies. It also leads continental Europe as a financial and insurance centre, according to the Global Financial Centres Index in 2026.
Many museums and art galleries can be found in the city, including the Swiss National Museum, Natural History Museum and Kunsthaus. Schauspielhaus Zürich is generally considered to be one of the most important theatres in the German-speaking world.
In German, the city name is written Zürich and pronounced ['tsyrç] . In the local dialect, the name is pronounced without the final consonant and with two short vowels, as Züri ['tsyri], although the demonym remains Zürcher(in). The city is called Zurich [zyik] in French, Zurigo [dzu'rio] in Italian, and Turitg [tu'rit]  in Romansh.
The earliest known form of the city's name is Turicum, attested on a tombstone of the late 2nd century AD in the form STA(tio) TURICEN(sis) ("Turicum customs post"). The name is interpreted as a derivation from a given name, possibly the Gaulish personal name Turos. The toponym *Turicon would then mean "belonging to Turos", "place of Turos". The Latin stress on the long vowel of the Gaulish name, [t'rikõ], was lost in German ['tsyrç] but is preserved in Italian [dzu'rio] and in Romansh [tu'rit].
The first development towards its later Germanic form is attested as early as c. 680–700 with the form Ziurichi. From the 9th century onward, the name is established in an Old High German form Zuri(c)h (857 in villa Zurih, 924 in Zurich curtem, 1416 Zürich Stadt).
